subject: dutchWindmill
pitch:
Category: Architecture.
Subject: Dutch windmill.
Style: Animal Crossing.
reasoning:
I'm planning a Dutch windmill model with a rotating sails joint, giving it a root "base" joint plus "cap" and "sails" joints so the blades can animate while the rest stays static.

I'm picturing a cute octagonal smock mill with a tapered white-plastered lower body, a rounded thatched cap with tail pole and fantail, four lattice-and-cloth sails, a balcony gallery, door, shuttered windows, and small props like flour sacks, kept proportionally scaled with a body around 9-10m tall and sail span near 10m.

I'm working out the geometry carefully so the sails clear the tapering tower walls — placing the windshaft hub far enough forward from the octagonal body (whose apothem narrows from about 3.0m at the base to 1.9m near the top) so the rotating sail plane sits safely in front of the front wall and gallery rail without clipping through the structure.

Now I'm sketching the joint hierarchy: a root mill joint at the origin, a cap joint around y=8.3 that could serve as the rotation hinge, and a windshaft joint positioned at the hub location, with the sails attached as children branching outward.

I'm working out the sail assembly itself, planning a fantail joint at the rear with its own axis, and designing each sail arm as a main stock beam with a lattice frame of slats attached to one side.

For the lattice look, I'm considering options like a cloth-and-wood texture or an SVG drawing, but deciding boxes for individual bars is the simplest reliable approach since extruded shapes with holes are tricky.

Planning each sail with roughly 16 parts: a stock beam, outer rail, about 12 crossbars, a couple diagonals, and a cloth panel near the bottom — times 4 sails that's around 64 parts, well within budget, so merging geometries isn't necessary. I'm now working out a helper function that computes each part's world position from hub location, angle, and radial/lateral/depth offsets, using z-rotation to orient each box along the sail arm.

Working out the rotation math so radial and lateral directions rotate correctly with angle theta, confirming the rotation-degrees convention applies, and planning to attach sail parts to a dedicated "sails" joint anchored at the hub so positions stay in model space.

Now I'm tackling the tower shape itself — using a lathe with 8 segments to create an octagonal taper, figuring out how the spin parameter and vertex radius versus apothem affect alignment, and trying to pin down which direction the first vertex faces by default.

For the paint scheme, I'm thinking of a brick base in warm terracotta with pale joints for the lower 2.2 meters, topped by a cream-white plastered octagon or golden-straw thatch upper body resembling traditional Dutch smock mills.

Writing custom paint function...

Mortar needs thickening, so I'll bump up to a larger paint sheet for better resolution. For the texture budget, I'm planning svg assets like windowpanes with crossbars, door planks, a nameplate emblem, and Dutch flower boxes with tulips planted at the base.

I want glowing warm light in the windows using the glow kit, but I'll skip toon shading since this style calls for soft pastel lighting instead — I'll handle warm-top cool-bottom lighting with my own paint logic. Now I'm sketching the overall structure in meters, defining the base height and tower body dimensions using lathe geometry for the brick base.

I'm working through the octagonal radius math for each tier — the brick base tapering from a wider bottom to a narrower top, then a gallery platform with railings, then the upper body tapering further toward the cap. I'm also checking whether the sail hub's lowest tip position might collide with the gallery platform's edge, since the radii are close enough to cause overlap.

I'll push the sail plane forward to z=4.6 with the hub there, keeping the frame depth around ±0.15, while the platform's apothem reaches 4.4 and the gallery's front edge sits at 4.2, with rail posts aligned there too.

Checking the windshaft length from the cap to the sail hub, I realize it protrudes quite a bit beyond the cap—maybe too long, so I'll shrink the sail radius to 5.8 and lower the hub height to 9.3, bringing the tip and rail top closer in for better proportions.

Now I'm shaping the cap: a boat-like thatched dome built from a lathed profile, with a skirt ring transitioning into a rounded top, and I'm considering whether to elongate it slightly along the z-axis to match the real Dutch cap's oval, boat-shaped silhouette.

Still writing lathe profile...

I'm setting up the cap's rotation hierarchy with joints for sails and fan as children of the cap bone, then moving to the body: an octagonal lathe with painted plank textures and separate corner post parts shaped as boxes or frustums along the edges.

Positioning rib posts just outside the faceted octagonal body at the vertex radius, then adding a couple of horizontal octagonal belt bands at mid and upper heights using closed polyline sweeps for structure. I also want to give the plaster walls a cream tone with subtle noise and warm top shading, then move on to the brick base detailing.

Now I'm defining the base construction: a lathed brick section with a wider grey stone plinth ring at the bottom touching the floor, followed by the main brick body profile, then a wooden cornice ledge transitioning into the upper body shape, and finally an octagonal gallery platform with planks at the base of the body.

For structural support, I'm considering slanted brace rods connecting the base wall to the platform's underside at each of the eight faces rather than full corbel brackets. I'm also working out door placement on the front face at ground level, since the gallery above sits too low to clear a standard door height, meaning access to the gallery would need a separate ladder or stair on the side.

I'm skipping a porch awning and instead adding a small two-step stoop with flour sacks beside the door, plus working out the geometry for an arched door texture on the tilted front face, calculating the wall's slope and radius at different heights to position the door plane correctly against the octagon's taper.

Defining helper functions for wall radius and face point positions, computing the face center at a given angle and height, offset outward along the normal direction.

Still writing wall helper...

I'm working out the normal tilt angle from the slope between radii, then planning how to orient plane geometries to face outward correctly. Now I'm thinking through window placement on the body faces — front-facing round-topped windows with shutters, diagonal faces with smaller upper windows, and glass textures with mullion patterns.

I'm thinking the hoist beam with a hanging rope and sack should sit at a diagonal front corner (around 45°), offset from the sails so they don't overlap, projecting outward from the wall near the cap.

Now I'm laying out the window placement around the mill's faces by angle — a large arched window on the front, smaller ones on the sides and diagonals, and maybe a round window at the back — along with where to put a name plaque reading "ANNO 1742."

For the stage rail, I'm planning an octagonal platform with posts at the vertices and mid-edges, placing frames around a closed loop path to position 16 posts evenly.

I also need to place stairs leading up to the gallery on the right side (a=-90), running along the platform edge where x is negative, with steps extending outward from the apothem face.

I'll make the stair a straight flight 1.0 wide centered at x=-4.75, running from z=-3.6 to a last step at z=-0.5 that abuts the platform edge, with 10 steps rising about 0.27 each to meet the platform top at 2.7, each step a solid box.

Each step has depth 0.38 and rises in increments to its own height, resting on the ground. I'm adding outer handrail posts and a sloped rail at x=-5.3, confirming the stairs stay clear of the sail plane. Then I'm designing the fantail: a tail pole extending back from the cap rear, angling slightly down, ending in a small eight-blade fan oriented to catch the wind.

Working out the fantail's orientation now — its rotor disc needs its normal along the x-axis, lying in the yz plane, so it catches crosswind and rotates the cap to face the main sails into the wind properly. I'm placing the fantail hub at roughly (0, 8.9, -5.6) with eight blades extruded as flat wedge boards rotated about x, supported by a frame of two beams extending back from the cap, and defining the tail pole as two rods running from the cap toward the fantail mount.

Checking for clearance between the rotor and the tower/gallery — the geometry seems fine since the rotor sits well behind the cap and tower at that height. Now I'm working out the yoke/axle structure connecting the tail pole to the hub, and figuring out how to compute each blade's pitch rotation using a quaternion combining the radial angle around x with a pitch tilt about the blade's own radial axis.

Writing basis-quaternion helper...

Still working out mill geometry...

Still placing lattice rails...

Adding two more thin longitudinal bars for the lattice grid, then thinking about adding a cream fabric panel near the tip of each arm, flag-style, maybe with red stripe accents.

I'm designing a sailcloth-style texture for the panel: cream fill with vertical stitched seams, dashed stitching lines, and a few darker patches, applied as a thin box so it shows on both faces, with all four arms getting this cloth treatment.

Counting up parts per arm (rails, cross-braces, longitudinal supports, cloth) brings each arm to roughly 19 pieces, about 76 total across four arms, plus the stocks. I'm picking warm brown tones for the lattice wood, with teal paint accents on the arm tips for a playful touch, and designing the hub as a cylindrical windshaft head with a cone nose cap.

Positioning the hub and windshaft rod, adding a red-orange spinner cone with a white band at the tip, and placing a cross-plate behind the hub to anchor the stocks through it. Still working out the cap's dome shape and ridge detailing.

For the apex I'm adding a small golden ball topped by a simple extruded arrow-shaped weathervane with a tail, keeping it cute and simple. I'm also defining a capProfile array to interpolate dome radius by height, so I can generate concentric thatch-course rings around the dome at increasing heights.

I'm sweeping darker golden-brown bands around the roof using closed catmull paths with twelve points each, adding about five bands for the thatch texture. For the lower rim, I'm giving it a scalloped reed-bundle hem by placing a ring of small flattened spheres along a closed path, using frame-based placement so each sphere follows the curve's orientation.

Since geometry attaches to whichever bone passes closest, and the cap joint's bone branches ambiguously toward the sails and fan, I'll explicitly pass the cap bone for all cap-related parts to avoid misassignment, and set up a helper function to simplify creating these parts.

Defining more joints...

Rather than posing the sails after assembly, I'll just build them tilted at around 18-20° from the start for that classic askew windmill look. Then I'm planning the front door — an arched plank design with iron hinges, sized roughly 1.15×1.9 and positioned at the base of the brick front.

I need to work out the entryway: a stoop with two steps leading up to the door, since the plinth itself sits about 0.55 high. I'm figuring out the geometry of the octagonal base so the steps, plinth ledge, and door plane all line up correctly at the front face.

Now I'm sizing the actual door opening (around 1.1×1.75, centered near y=1.43) so it fits cleanly below the cornice line, and planning a stone frame plate plus a small canopy or lintel with a keystone above it, with lanterns flanking the door for a bit of warm glow.

I'm also working out the porch steps as stacked boxes — figuring dimensions and z-positions for two overlapping stair boxes so they sit properly in front of the plinth without clipping through it.

Then I'm placing the gallery platform and its support braces at the octagon's vertices rather than face centers, so they clear the doorway below. I'm also carving out a gap in the platform rail for the stair opening on the back face.

I'm checking that the rail placement sits slightly inset from the platform vertices, comparing the apothem to the vertex radius, and confirming the rail height at the mid-arm area doesn't clash with the lattice or sail geometry at that vertex angle.

Now I'm working through stock depth, lattice offset, and cap sizing relative to the body's top octagon, making sure the cap overhangs the body appropriately with a darker skirt ring for contrast. I'm also starting to define the color palette for brick tones, mortar, and plaster.

Defining more colors...

Still defining paint helpers...

Estimating total painted area around 300m², which gives a texture density near 99 texels per meter at 2048 resolution. For the plaster body I'm planning cream coloring with subtle noise mottling, vertical plank seam lines every 0.35m, and a darker grey dirt band near the bottom fading to a lighter cream/peach near the top for a worn but clean look.

For the thatch cap I'm adding straw coloring with vertical stalk streaks, darker course lines every 0.3m in height with a lighter band above each, plus scattered green moss patches using noise thresholding near the top. For the platform I'm laying out wood planks along the x-axis using floor division on position, with the top face getting a flat wood tone when the surface normal points upward.

For the stone plinth I'm using a patches function with a base gray tone and lighter speckled variants to create a rough stone texture. Lighting will rely on standard material shading from the lights, with the painted colors providing warm/cool tonal variation baked directly into flat colors.

Now I'm planning the SVG textures I'll need: an arched window with glass, mullions, and a warm glow with transparent cutaway corners; an arched plank door with hinges and a handle; a plaque reading "ANNO 1742"; sailcloth texture; and tulip card variants in red, yellow, and pink.

For the tulips, I'm designing a single grayscale tulip drawing with petals and shading that gets tinted by a color parameter, building a small tulipSvg function that takes petal and shade colors so I can reuse it cheaply for each variant. I'm also sketching a teal shutter texture with vertical plank lines and a heart-shaped cutout decal, applied to thin boxes where the texture shows through on all faces. Finally I'm considering a sack texture, possibly using a small label card to suggest a flour sack.

I'm deciding to skip extra decorative ideas like flags, clocks, and gable windows to keep things focused, settling on the current texture list: window, door, plaque, cloth, shutter, tulips, and sack label, plus glow effects for windows and lanterns. For the window shapes, I'm working out an arched-top frame using an extruded outline built from a semicircular polyline combined with the rectangular base.

Still writing extrusion math...

For the window shape itself, I'm defining an arch-outline helper that builds the rectangular sides plus a curved top using a handful of arc points, and I need the glass pane to follow that same arched silhouette rather than staying rectangular.

Working out the layering now: the frame extrudes slightly larger than the opening and sits recessed into the wall, while the glass plane floats just in front of it with a small gap so they don't visually clash.

Now I'm sizing the shutters as flat boxes flanking the window with their own SVG texture, matching the window's bottom edge, and starting to add a wooden flower box beneath the sill.

Still writing card placement logic... I should also add a bed of tulips along the base, patches at the front of the plinth with rows of tulips and leaves.

Each sack is a tied cream sphere shape with a small label plane. I'm adjusting positions so the tulip planters, sacks, and stoop don't collide — shifting planters out to ±2.6 and sacks to roughly ±1.25 to keep clearance from the stoop edges.

Now I'm adding wall-mounted lanterns beside the door, each built from a small glowing box, a pyramid cap, and a bracket rod, positioned around x=±1.0 so they clear the door frame. Next I'm working out the window placements by checking the front wall's body geometry.

For the windows themselves, I'm planning a large arched window on the front face, with a plaque above it and possibly a hatch near the top. I'm also considering a diagonal loading door with a wooden hatch texture, plus a hoist beam projecting outward with a brace, pulley, and hanging sack above it.

Now I'm placing smaller windows at the 45°, 90°, -90°, and 135° angles around the mill, with round glowing windows for the diagonal faces, and reconsidering the loading hatch height so it sits just above the gallery platform rail rather than overlapping it.

I'm also figuring out door placement at the -90° angle where the stairs land on the gallery platform, pairing it with a window above, then filling in the remaining symmetric windows at 90° and 180° to keep the facade balanced.

Now I'm checking the body wall's slight tilt angle and realizing the window frames need adjustment since the wall recedes slightly from bottom to top of each opening — the vertical frame extrusion would otherwise create a gap from the wall surface, so I need a better way to embed them flush.

I verify the dot product confirms orthogonality between the tangent and normal vectors, so extruding along the tangent and up-vector gives the correct wall normal. I'm setting up a wall type definition and a helper function to compute the face geometry consistently for both the extruded walls and the plane elements like glass.

Since faces are flat, lateral movement on a face is just true tangential motion, confirming the approach works. I'm checking that DEG is properly exported from the math module, and computing the slight tilt factor for the brick base using the wall's radius values at y0 and y1.

Now I'm working out the lathe profile for the body section — matching radii between the wall and lathe at the transition point around y=2.6, adjusting r0 to roughly 3.12 so the door placement (which sits above y=2.78) stays clear. The platform spanning y 2.45–2.7 covers the body's bottom edge nicely, and the cap skirt begins where the body joins at y=8.0, with the hoist positioned on the 45-degree face around y=6.

For the hoist itself, I'm keeping it simple: a wooden beam projecting outward from the face at y=6.8, braced diagonally down to the lower wall at y=5.9, with a rope hanging down to about y=5.0 and a sack dangling near y=4.75, offset roughly 1.6 units out from the wall. Since the hatch sits between y=3.1 and 4.6 on that face, the sack ends up hovering just in front of the hatch's upper edge, which should read fine visually without colliding with any windows.

Now I'm working out the lathe geometry details — using an `at` origin of [0,0,0], building closed profile outlines along the x-axis (x≥0) that go out and back to form the cap and platform shapes, and setting segment counts (8 for lower shading to stay flat-faced, 14 for the cap) to control how smooth or faceted the rotation looks, while making sure sharp profile corners still crease properly.

I'm settling on 10 segments for the cap to keep a faceted low-poly look consistent with the octagon theme, and noting that lathe paint heights correspond to absolute y-values in the outline. Then I move to sweep and rod calls for the shorter posts, defining their path points and radius options.

For boxes I plan to use the plain BoxGeometry parts since they're naturally flat-faced, and for textured planes I set up direction, axis, and up vectors alongside a texture option. I also note that glow effects fail on parts using the "paint" material name, but textured flat-color parts should still work fine.

Now I'm sorting out imports and types for the TypeScript build—sticking to safe SDK exports like createBuilder, frame, rng, polyline, catmull, paint, patches, noise, mix, smoothstep, svg, and DEG, while avoiding risky type imports by deriving joint types with ReturnType and defining my own simple color type instead of importing Rgb directly.

Setting up imports and constants...

Still writing color conversion logic...

Checking mortar gap dimensions, they look reasonable in real-world scale. For brick coloring I'm mixing two base colors with a hash function per row/column plus noise, adding mossy green near the bottom for weathering, darkening toward the base, then applying lighting based on surface normal with special handling for top faces.

Looking at the seam problem, the column count around the cylinder doesn't divide evenly, causing a mismatch where bricks wrap -- so I'm switching to 64 columns to keep things seamless, recalculating column width and mortar gap accordingly. Now I'm writing the plaster paint function for the main body.

Still writing texture shaders...

Writing deck planks and stone plinth paint...

Designing the glass window shape...

Working out the pane dimensions and centering math, then moving to the frame outline margins and starting the door texture's arched plank design.

Writing door plank code...

Then I'm planning the plaque details—brass lettering reading "ANNO 1742" on a dark wood board with small tulip decorations flanking the text.

Now moving to the sailcloth design: a cream canvas with vertical stitched seams, dashed stitching lines, hemmed edges, and a small red appliqué patch for visual interest, before sketching out the shutter element in teal.

I'm parameterizing the tulip colors into three variations (red, yellow, pink) and adding leaf tuft textures for the planter fill, plus a simple flour sack label with text. That brings the texture list up to window, door, plaque, cloth, shutter, three tulip variants, and leaves.

Now I'm starting the build function itself, setting up the joint hierarchy for the windmill: a root "mill" joint, a cap joint above it, sail and fantail hubs positioned off the cap, working through how the directional vectors should orient each bone.

Setting up helper functions...

Still writing lathe profiles...

I realize the platform's solid lathe shape (2.45–2.7) already covers the gap between brick top and body start, so the separate cornice piece is unnecessary. Now I'm defining the body lathe profile from 2.6 to 8.0 with plaster, spinning in 8 segments, and sketching a platform lathe profile with a deck-painted rim from 2.42 to 2.7.

Next I'm placing corner posts along the body's vertex angles, computing their radius as a function of height and extending them from y=2.7 up to 7.95 with a small radial offset and wood-toned color. Then I'm planning belt rings as closed polylines at a few height levels, swept with rounded cross-sections at the vertex radii plus a small offset to sit just outside the body surface.

For the platform structure, I'm defining vertex positions as a function of index, radius, and height, then working out rail edges between consecutive vertices using the midpoint angle of each face to figure out which edge corresponds to the staircase gap (at 270°, matching k=5), so I can skip rails and posts there to leave an opening.

Now I'm placing the rails and posts at the correct heights and radii, and accounting for the stair geometry - ten steps with a fixed center x-position and width, stepping down in z to connect smoothly with the platform edge opening I identified.

Reworking the stair orientation so it runs parallel to the platform edge rather than perpendicular, meaning the climber turns sideways at the top to step onto the platform. I'm computing each step's z-center and verifying the top step lands at y=2.7, then adding a small landing box to bridge into the platform.

I'm also planning a landing deck with support posts rather than a solid filled block, adjusting widths so the landing overlaps the platform edge and the stair treads align with the platform radius. Finally I'm sketching a sloped handrail with posts spaced every few steps down to the base.

For the railings, I'm mapping vertex coordinates on the platform polygon to connect the landing's outer rail to adjacent vertices, closing the gap at the opening between roughly z=-1.7 and z=1.7, while keeping the stair rail segment separate from the post near vertex 5.

Now I'm defining a door on the body's -90° face, sizing it 0.9×1.6 with an arched top aligned to the platform surface, then moving into a helper function for placing windows with optional shutters and box frames.

Finishing the frame extrusion: it's a trim-colored frame slightly larger than the window opening, offset outward from the wall, with the glass pane positioned a touch further out in front of the frame.

Finishing the arch outline function...

I'm checking constraints so the arc stays valid, confirming heights exceed radii for both frames and windows, and sketching dimensions for doors, window frames, and straight-sided shutter boxes.

The shutters sit flush at a fixed offset from the bottom, extrusion uses the default upward axis, and the low-segment arch outline stays intentionally faceted for a low-poly look. For the glass panes, I'm placing a plane geometry scaled to the window proportions, aligned to the wall's normal and up vectors, textured, and then adding a glow pass on top.

Then I'm positioning paired shutters laterally on each side of the window using small thin boxes with their own texture, followed by a stone-colored sill box beneath the frame, and starting to set up an optional flower box attachment for certain windows.

Writing planter box and tulip cards...

Now I'm sketching a plaque near the top with a gold wooden frame behind it, then working on the front door dimensions — an arched opening sized to the plinth height, roughly 1.1 wide by 1.8 tall.

I'm detailing the door frame outline with a cream stone lintel color and adding a keystone accent at the arch peak, deciding against a glow texture for simplicity. I considered adding a small porch hood or wedge-shaped awning above the door but decided to skip it in favor of keeping the entrance plain.

Now I'm placing lanterns on either side of the wall using bracket rods extending outward, with glowing lantern bodies and spike caps mounted on the brackets. I'm also sketching out a loading hatch at a 45-degree angle, planning to reuse a wood-plank door texture with cross braces for the hatch panel.

Settling on an open hatch look with a dark extruded arch hole for the interior, then moving on to add a hoist beam above it on the body face.

Still placing the beam geometry...

Now I'm defining a sack-placement helper that creates scaled spheres with a tie knot and a front-facing label, plus starting the lathe profile for a cap shape with a sequence of radius/height control points.

Checking that the cap's profile loop closes properly back along the axis, then setting lathe segment and spin counts. I'm figuring out the cap's hub radius at its windshaft mounting height and planning a small protruding hood or snout where the shaft exits the front.

Writing nose lathe profile...

Now defining the windshaft rod, iron neck bands, and tail beam bracing for the rear of the cap with their positions and dimensions.

Still working out the fan assembly geometry...

I realize the beam actually sits right inside the rotor's swept circle, so the blades would clip through it as they spin — real fantails avoid this by keeping the support frame outside the rotor plane, so I need to rethink the geometry so the beam doesn't intersect the blade disc.

I'll shift the two frame beams to x=±0.55 so they pass outside the blade disc, running from the cap rear back to the hub, with a cross brace and diagonal supports connecting them. Then I'm positioning the eight fan blades around the hub at radius 1.4, each as a thin angled box.

For the thatched cap, I'm layering rings at increasing heights with radii interpolated from the roof profile, using small circular cross-sections in warm thatch colors, then adding a scalloped hem of flattened sphere "reed bundles" arranged around the lower rim to give it a textured, woven look.

Now I'm designing the finial topper: a gilded sphere at the apex with a spike rod rising above it, plus a simple arrow-shaped wind vane outlined as a small 2D profile mounted sideways near the top of the spike.

Confirming it's a valid simple polygon traced counterclockwise, then extruding it along the z-axis with a thin red vane shape mounted at the cap top, plus adding small round dormer windows on the cap sides.

Computing the oculus normal direction from the lathe slope at that height, then moving on to the sails section with a hub position defined and a helper function for placing sail points by angle, latitude, radius, and depth.

Still defining the stock geometry...

Still placing sail boxes...

Adding the hub drum with a cream band, then the nose cone with a gilt ball tip, before moving to the fan rotor mounted at the rear with alternating red and cream blades.

I'll make the rims out of wood tone rather than teal, skip extra bunting and flags for now, and skip a chimney since the plinth base already works. For the front, I'm placing small planter boxes on either side with soil beds for a grid of tulip cards, positioning them symmetrically with slightly lower dark brown soil layers beneath.

Now I'm setting up the tulip frames and leaf cards using the texture system with randomized orientation, and considering whether to add extra tulip clumps at the base corners before deciding to skip that detail. I'm tallying up the rough part count across the whole structure—lathes, posts, belts, braces, railings, stairs, windows with their frames and shutters, the door, lanterns, and planters—to get a sense of the model's total complexity.

Adding soil box and tulip frame positions...

I'm planning to collect all tulip and leaf frames into arrays and batch the cards calls at the end for efficiency, then setting up the door frame on the brick wall with its wall parameters and arch dimensions.

I'm adding the tie at the top of each sack using a small sphere and cone for the ruffle, plus a flattened sphere for a ribbon band, and placing a front-facing label plane with "SACK" text texture positioned near the top of the sack.

Checking how `b.cards` works with frame arrays and the `rng(seed)` helper for randomized card placement, confirming no color tinting is needed, and sizing the tulip texture cards to match a 32:64 drawing aspect ratio.

Confirming glow placement matches expected part types and that `bone` defaults are joint-compatible, then moving on to setting up the color palette constants for the brickwork, mortar, trim, and plaster materials.

Writing palette constants...

Setting up joints...

Rod should accept sides as a sweep shorthand option, and closed ring tubes using closed polylines should skip caps fine. I'm planning the platform deck using lathe with proper paint and naming, then moving on to the face geometry next.
